key: The Gods seek him who presses out the Soma; they desire not sleep They punish sloth unweariedly.
s: Amid the Kanvas’ call to Indra, the hymn turns to the gods and the worshipper; Sāyaṇa, on 8.2.18, reads it as the gods, wishing to guard the presser, keeping him ever awake, and takes the word rendered ‘sloth’ as the gladdening Soma they tirelessly reach.

evidence.gloss: The gods, Indra and all the rest, wish to protect the sacrificer who presses the Soma. They do not desire sleep: they do not want the state of sleep for that presser; the sense is that they always keep him awake. (A grammatical note on the dative.) Since this is so, the unwearied, unslothful gods reach pramāda, that is, his Soma, which gladdens exceedingly.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Rig Veda 8.2.18 at [621,18], matching the proposal). The packet’s Sanskrit verse (icchanti devāḥ sunvantaṃ na svapnāya spṛhayanti, yanti pramādam atandrāḥ) is the app’s 8.2.18. Sāyaṇa glosses: the gods wish to protect the presser, do not want sleep for him and keep him always awake, and the unwearied gods reach pramāda, which he takes as the exceedingly gladdening Soma; Griffith’s ‘sloth’ renders pramāda. Wilson (vol. 4, packet) follows him: ‘they, unslothful, obtain the inebriating Soma’. Plain sense faithful: 8.2 is to Indra, the Kanvas praise him (16, 22, 38), and 17 and 19 address Indra while 18 speaks of the gods and the presser; no four-word run from the key.
